lessons.lessonTitle: Lesson 1: Destructuring, Spread/Rest Operators, and Modules

options: `1 undefined [4, 5]`
questions.explanation: `a` takes index 0 (`1`), index 1 is skipped, `b` encounters `undefined` and takes default value `10`, and `rest` collects remaining elements `[4, 5]`.

questions.question: How can you swap the values of two variables `x` and `y` in a single line without using a temporary variable?
options: swap(x, y);
x, y = y, x;
questions.explanation: Array destructuring assignment `[x, y] = [y, x];` creates a temporary array with `[y, x]` and immediately unpacks the swapped values into `x` and `y`.

options: "Alex ['twitter', 'github']"
"Alex github"
"undefined github"
"Alex twitter"
questions.explanation: `name` extracts `'Alex'`, and `[, secondSocial]` skips the first element of `socials` and assigns index 1 (`'github'`) to `secondSocial`.

options: "undefined:undefined"
"localhost:8080"
TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined
questions.explanation: The outer default `= {}` ensures that calling `connect()` without arguments defaults to an empty object, allowing the inner destructuring defaults `host = 'localhost'` and `port = 8080` to apply.

options: "dark false"
"light false"
"blue true"
"blue false"
questions.explanation: Object spreading merges properties from left to right; `userPref` is spread last, overriding `theme` with `'light'` and `showSidebar` with `false`.

questions.question: How do ES Modules (ESM) handle exported variable bindings compared to CommonJS (`require()`)?
options: Both module systems export immutable binary strings
ES Modules export live bindings (mutations in the exporting module are reflected dynamically in importers), while CommonJS exports static value copies
CommonJS exports live bindings, while ES Modules export frozen snapshots
ES Modules do not allow exporting variables, only classes
questions.explanation: ESM exports live bindings (if an exported variable changes inside the module, imported references see the updated value in real time). CommonJS copies the value at require time.

questions.question: What is the difference between Named Exports and Default Exports in ES Modules?
options: Named exports must be written in uppercase, while default exports are lowercase
Default exports cannot be imported in web browsers
Default exports are asynchronous, while named exports are synchronous
A module can have multiple Named Exports imported using matching `{ name }` syntax, but only ONE Default Export per file imported without curly braces using any custom identifier
questions.explanation: You can export multiple named items (`export const A = 1, B = 2;` $\rightarrow$ `import { A, B }`) but only one default export (`export default MyClass;` $\rightarrow$ `import AnyName from ...`).

questions.question: What does the dynamic import syntax `import('./analytics.js')` return?
options: The exported default object synchronously
An HTML `<script>` DOM element
A Promise that resolves to the module namespace object containing all exports
A boolean indicating if the file was found on the server
questions.explanation: Dynamic `import(path)` returns a Promise, enabling code splitting and on-demand lazy loading of JavaScript modules at runtime.

questions.question: How do you re-export all exports from an authentication module `auth.js` in an `index.js` barrel file?
options: module.exports = require('./auth.js');
import * as auth from './auth.js'; export default auth;
export * from './auth.js';
export.all('./auth.js');
questions.explanation: `export * from './auth.js'` re-exports all named exports from the target module, creating clean public barrel entry points.

questions.question: What feature did ES2022 standardize regarding `await` in top-level module code?
options: `await` can only be used inside `for` loops
Top-level await pauses all other browser tabs simultaneously
`await` was deprecated in favor of callback functions
Top-Level Await: `await` can be used directly at the top level of an ES module without wrapping inside an `async` function
questions.explanation: Top-Level Await allows ES modules to act as async module initializers (e.g., awaiting database connections or config fetches before exporting).

options: TypeError: Cannot assign to read only property
undefined
99 (Because the spread operator only creates a shallow copy, leaving nested objects shared by reference)
2 (Because `copy` is a completely independent clone)
questions.explanation: Object spread `{ ...original }` is shallow; `copy.nested` holds the same memory address as `original.nested`, so modifying `copy.nested.b` mutates `original.nested.b`.

questions.question: How do you rename an imported named export `fetchData` to `getUserData` to prevent naming collisions?
options: import { fetchData as getUserData } from './api.js';
import { fetchData -> getUserData } from './api.js';
import { fetchData: getUserData } from './api.js';
import { getUserData = fetchData } from './api.js';
questions.explanation: In ES module import/export statements, the `as` keyword is used for aliasing (e.g., `import { name as alias } from ...`).

questions.question: What is `import.meta` in ES Modules?
options: A meta-property object exposing context-specific metadata about the current module (such as `import.meta.url`)
A built-in Redux state management object
A method that imports HTML `<meta>` tags into JavaScript
A compiler directive that optimizes V8 JIT compilation
questions.explanation: `import.meta` contains metadata about the current module, such as its URL (`import.meta.url`), environment flags, or bundler-specific variables.

questions.question: What will `[...'Hello']` evaluate to in JavaScript?
options: ['Hello']
TypeError: String is not an array
questions.explanation: Strings are iterable; spreading a string into an array literal `[...str]` spreads its characters as individual elements.

options: 'score'
ReferenceError: key is not defined
undefined
questions.explanation: Computed property destructuring `{ [key]: result }` evaluates `key` (`'score'`) and assigns `player['score']` (100) to the variable `result`.

questions.question: Why does `"use strict";` not need to be declared inside an ES Module file (`<script type="module">`)?
options: Strict mode is only supported in CommonJS
All ES Modules are executed in Strict Mode by default automatically
Modern browsers deprecated strict mode in 2020
ES Modules do not support Strict Mode
questions.explanation: According to the ECMAScript specification, module code is always parsed and executed in Strict Mode automatically.

questions.question: What is the output of `const obj = { a: 1, b: 2 }; const { a, ...rest } = obj; console.log(rest);`?
options: undefined
questions.explanation: Object rest destructuring `{ a, ...rest }` extracts `a` and collects all remaining own enumerable properties into a new plain object `{ b: 2 }`.

questions.question: Which of the following is true about how ES Modules are loaded in HTML documents (`<script type="module" src="app.js">`)?
options: Module scripts can only execute after `window.onload` fires
Module scripts block HTML parsing synchronously like regular scripts
Module scripts cannot import external NPM packages
Module scripts are automatically deferred by default (non-blocking download, executing after HTML parsing completes)
questions.explanation: `<script type="module">` scripts are deferred by default, loading in parallel with HTML parsing and executing in document order once the DOM is parsed.

questions.question: What is the result of using the spread operator with `Math.max()` on an array `const numbers = [4, 18, 3, 92, 11];`?
options: Math.max(...numbers) evaluates to 92
Math.max(numbers) evaluates to 92
Math.max(...numbers) evaluates to NaN
Math.max(...numbers) evaluates to [92]
questions.explanation: `Math.max()` expects individual numeric arguments; `Math.max(...numbers)` spreads the array into arguments `Math.max(4, 18, 3, 92, 11)` and returns `92`.

questions.question: What happens if an ES Module has circular dependencies (e.g., module A imports module B, and module B imports module A)?
options: All circular imports are converted to `null` automatically
The JavaScript engine crashes with an unrecoverable stack overflow error immediately
ESM supports circular dependencies via live bindings, but accessing uninitialized imports in the TDZ before declaration will throw a `ReferenceError`
The browser refuses to load any scripts on the page
questions.explanation: ES Modules handle circular references gracefully via live binding references, though care must be taken not to access TDZ bindings before they are evaluated.

lessons.lessonTitle: Lesson 2: Promises, Async/Await, and Fetch API Integration

questions.explanation: Synchronous code runs first (`1, 4`). Promise `.then()` callbacks enter the Microtask Queue and execute before the Macrotask Queue (`3`). `setTimeout` enters the Macrotask Queue and executes last (`2`).

questions.question: What are the three possible mutual lifecycle states of a JavaScript `Promise`?
options: `active`, `paused`, `stopped`
`waiting`, `completed`, `failed`
`pending`, `fulfilled`, `rejected`
`initialized`, `resolved`, `terminated`
questions.explanation: A Promise starts in `pending` and transitions immutably to either `fulfilled` (with a value) or `rejected` (with an error reason).

questions.question: What happens when you return a plain value (e.g., `return 42;`) from inside a `.then()` callback in a Promise chain?
options: The returned value is ignored and `undefined` is passed to the next `.then()`
The `.then()` method returns a new Promise that immediately resolves to the returned value (`42`)
It throws a `TypeError: Cannot return non-promise from .then`
The Promise chain terminates immediately
questions.explanation: Any value returned from a `.then()` handler is automatically wrapped in `Promise.resolve(value)`, allowing seamless method chaining.

questions.question: How does `Promise.all([p1, p2, p3])` behave if `p2` rejects with an error while `p1` and `p3` are still pending?
options: It converts the error into an empty object `{}`
It returns `[p1_result, null, p3_result]`
It rejects immediately with `p2`'s rejection error (fail-fast behavior), ignoring the results of other pending promises
It waits for `p1` and `p3` to complete and ignores `p2`'s error
questions.explanation: `Promise.all()` is all-or-nothing: if any single promise rejects, the entire `Promise.all()` immediately rejects with that first rejection reason.

questions.question: What is the primary advantage of `Promise.allSettled([p1, p2, p3])` over `Promise.all()`?
options: It runs promises on multi-threaded GPU cores

It never short-circuits on rejection; it waits for ALL promises to settle and returns an array of objects describing each outcome (`{ status: 'fulfilled', value }` or `{ status: 'rejected', reason }`)
It retries failed promises up to 5 times automatically
It only works with HTTP GET requests
questions.explanation: `Promise.allSettled()` guarantees all asynchronous tasks finish, giving detailed reports for every promise regardless of success or failure.

questions.question: What is the difference between `Promise.race()` and `Promise.any()`?
options: There is no difference; both are exact aliases
`Promise.any()` returns all values, while `Promise.race()` returns one
`Promise.race()` only works with timers, while `Promise.any()` is for fetch
`Promise.race()` settles with the first settled promise (whether fulfilled OR rejected), while `Promise.any()` settles with the first FULFILLED promise (ignoring rejections until all fail)
questions.explanation: `Promise.race()` takes the very first result (even if it's an error). `Promise.any()` seeks the first success; if all reject, it rejects with an `AggregateError`.

questions.question:
Why does the following Fetch API code fail to catch HTTP 404 and 500 errors in the `.catch()` block? 
```javascript
fetch('https://api.example.com/not-found')
  .then(res => res.json())
  .catch(err => console.log('Error caught!'));
```
options: The `fetch()` Promise only rejects on network failures or blocked requests; HTTP error statuses (404, 500) resolve normally and require checking `response.ok` manually
The URL must end in `.json` for errors to trigger `.catch()`
HTTP 404 is considered a successful response by all web protocols
`fetch()` does not support `.catch()` method chaining
questions.explanation: `fetch()` treats HTTP 4xx and 5xx responses as successful HTTP communications. Developers must inspect `if (!res.ok) throw new Error(res.statusText);` to trigger catch blocks.

questions.question: What is the correct syntax to send a JSON payload in an HTTP POST request using the Fetch API?
options: fetch(url, { method: 'POST', data: data });
fetch.post(url, JSON.toPayload(data));
fetch(url, { method: 'POST', headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' }, body: JSON.stringify(data) });
fetch(url, { bodyType: 'json', payload: data });
questions.explanation: Standard Fetch POST requires setting `method: 'POST'`, providing `headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' }`, and passing a stringified payload to `body`.

questions.question: How do you implement a 5-second request timeout for a `fetch()` call using `AbortController`?
options: fetch(url).setTimeout(5000);
const c = new AbortController(); fetch(url, { cancelAfter: 5000 });
fetch(url, { timeout: 5000 });
const c = new AbortController(); setTimeout(() => c.abort(), 5000); fetch(url, { signal: c.signal });
questions.explanation: Binding `signal: controller.signal` to `fetch()` allows aborting the pending HTTP request when `controller.abort()` is called via `setTimeout`.

questions.question: What does an `async` function always return in JavaScript?
options: A Promise (wrapping the returned value in `Promise.resolve` or rejections in `Promise.reject`)
A callback function
A generator iterator object
The raw synchronous value directly
questions.explanation: Functions declared with `async` always return a Promise, even if you write `return 42;` (which returns `Promise.resolve(42)`).

options: Approach A executes requests sequentially in series (total time = A + B), while Approach B executes both requests concurrently in parallel (total time = max(A, B))
Approach A is faster because it uses less network bandwidth
Approach B is invalid syntax in modern JavaScript
Both approaches take identical execution time
questions.explanation: Awaiting promises sequentially forces `getP()` to wait until `getU()` finishes. Using `Promise.all()` starts both requests concurrently in parallel, slashing total wait time.

questions.question: How do you handle errors properly in an `async/await` function?
options: Use `.catch()` on every variable name
Async functions cannot throw errors
Wrap the `await` expressions in a `try...catch` block
Set `window.errorHandling = 'async';`
questions.explanation: Rejected promises awaited inside an `async` function throw exceptions, which can be cleanly intercepted using standard synchronous-like `try...catch` blocks.

questions.question: What is Microtask Queue Starvation in JavaScript?
options: When the browser runs out of cookies
A CPU hardware bug on mobile smartphones
A memory leak caused by unclosed IndexedDB connections
Continuously scheduling microtasks (e.g., recursive `Promise.resolve().then(...)` or `queueMicrotask`) without returning control, starving macrotasks, UI rendering, and user input
questions.explanation: The event loop processes all pending microtasks before rendering or checking macrotasks; an unending chain of microtasks starves the event loop and locks up UI rendering.

questions.question: What happens if an `async` function throws an unhandled exception?
options: The returned Promise is rejected with the thrown error
The error is converted into an empty string
The function returns `null` silently
The browser terminates JavaScript execution across all tabs
questions.explanation: Throwing inside an `async` function (e.g., `throw new Error('fail');`) causes the function's returned Promise to reject with that error.

questions.question: Which Response method is used to extract the binary image or file payload from a Fetch request?
options: response.blob() (or response.arrayBuffer())
response.image()
response.toFile()
response.binary()
questions.explanation: `response.blob()` resolves to a `Blob` object representing raw binary data (ideal for images, PDFs, or media downloads).

options: Promise { 'Result' }
"Result"
TypeError: test(...).then is not a function
undefined
questions.explanation: `test()` returns a Promise resolving to `'Result'`; `.then()` receives the resolved string `'Result'`.

questions.question: What global event listener captures unhandled Promise rejections in modern web browsers?
options: document.onreject = handler;
window.addEventListener('unhandledrejection', event => { console.log(event.reason); });
window.addEventListener('promiseerror', handler);
window.addEventListener('async:error', handler);
questions.explanation: The `unhandledrejection` event fires on `window` whenever a Promise rejects without an attached `.catch()` handler.

questions.question: What does `queueMicrotask(() => { ... })` do?
options: It creates a background Web Worker thread
It schedules a function to run 1 hour in the future
It queues a task to be processed on the backend server
It explicitly enqueues a callback into the Microtask Queue, executing it immediately after the current synchronous script and before rendering or macrotasks
questions.explanation: `queueMicrotask()` provides a standardized API to schedule microtask callbacks with higher priority than `setTimeout(fn, 0)` without Promise instantiation overhead.

questions.question: What is the return value of `Promise.resolve(5).then(x => x * 2).then(x => { throw new Error('err'); }).catch(e => 100).then(x => x + 1)`?
options: UnhandledPromiseRejection
101 (The `.catch()` handler catches the error, recovers by returning 100, and passes 100 to the next `.then()` which computes 100 + 1)
NaN
questions.explanation: Errors skip intermediate `.then()` handlers until reaching `.catch()`. The `.catch()` returns `100` (recovering the chain), which flows into the subsequent `.then(x => x + 1)` to yield `101`.

questions.question: Why should `await` NOT be used inside a traditional `Array.prototype.forEach()` loop?
options: `forEach` throws a syntax error if `await` is inside its callback
`forEach` can only process synchronous integers
`forEach` converts all promises into numbers automatically
`forEach` does not wait for async callback promises to resolve, running all iterations concurrently without waiting and ignoring returned promises
questions.explanation: `forEach` is synchronous and ignores the Promises returned by async callbacks. For sequential async loops, use `for (const item of array)` with `await`.

lessons.lessonTitle: Lesson 3: Handling JSON Data & Dynamic API Integrations

questions.question: Which of the following represents a valid JSON string according to RFC 8259 specifications?
options: {"name": "Alice", "date": new Date()}
{"name": "Alice", "age": 25, "active": true, "roles": ["admin"]}
{ 'name': 'Alice', 'age': 25, }
{ name: "Alice", age: 25 }
questions.explanation: JSON strictly requires double quotes around property keys and string values, prohibits trailing commas, and disallows JavaScript expressions/constructors like `new Date()`.

questions.question: What happens when `JSON.stringify()` encounters an object containing a function, `undefined`, and a Symbol property?
options: It omits all three properties from the serialized JSON string output
It converts all three into empty strings `""`
It converts the function into executable text and keeps undefined
It throws a fatal `TypeError`
questions.explanation: `JSON.stringify()` omits functions, `undefined`, and Symbols when serializing objects (or converts them to `null` if encountered inside an array).

questions.question: How can you safely format a JSON string with 2-space indentation for human readability?
options: JSON.stringify(data, 'indent: 2');
JSON.stringify(data).indent(2);
JSON.stringify(data, null, 2);
JSON.format(data, 2);
questions.explanation: The third argument of `JSON.stringify(value, replacer, space)` controls whitespace indentation (passing `2` formats with 2 spaces).

questions.question: How do you parse a JSON string containing an ISO date string (e.g., `'{"createdAt": "2026-09-11T12:00:00Z"}'`) and automatically restore it as a real JavaScript `Date` object?
options: Set `JSON.parseDates = true;` before parsing
Use `JSON.parse(jsonStr, { parseDates: true });`
JSON parses dates automatically without extra code
Use a reviver function: `JSON.parse(jsonStr, (key, value) => key === 'createdAt' ? new Date(value) : value);`
questions.explanation: The reviver callback in `JSON.parse(text, reviver)` transforms each key-value pair during parsing, allowing strings matching date patterns to be instantiated as `Date` objects.

questions.question: Why should `JSON.parse()` almost always be wrapped in a `try...catch` block when processing API responses or localStorage data?
options: Because invalid, malformed, or empty JSON strings throw a fatal `SyntaxError` that will crash the application if uncaught
Because `try...catch` accelerates JSON parsing speed by 50%
Because valid JSON is automatically deleted from memory unless caught
Because `JSON.parse()` triggers network requests behind the scenes
questions.explanation: Malformed JSON (or empty strings) causes `JSON.parse()` to throw a synchronous `SyntaxError: Unexpected token...`, making `try-catch` error handling essential.

questions.question: If an object has a custom `.toJSON()` method defined, how does `JSON.stringify()` treat that object?
options: It calls the `.toJSON()` method and serializes whatever value `.toJSON()` returns instead of serializing the raw object
It ignores the `.toJSON()` method completely
It throws a TypeError for conflicting methods
It deletes the object from the DOM
questions.explanation: If an object defines a `toJSON()` method, `JSON.stringify()` delegates serialization to that method (which is how `Date.prototype.toJSON()` formats ISO date strings).

questions.question: When uploading a file using Fetch and `FormData`, why is it an anti-pattern to manually set `headers: { 'Content-Type': 'multipart/form-data' }`?
options: Manually setting the header omits the required `boundary` parameter string, causing the backend server to fail to parse the multipart payload
Because `FormData` is encrypted with SSL automatically
Because `FormData` only works with `Content-Type: application/json`
Because browsers reject all POST requests with custom headers
questions.explanation: When passing `body: new FormData()`, the browser automatically sets `Content-Type: multipart/form-data; boundary=----WebKitFormBoundary...`. Manually setting it strips the boundary delimiter, breaking server parsing.

questions.question: What is an 'Optimistic UI Update' pattern in web API applications?
options: Disabling all error logging in production builds
Assuming the user's internet connection will never fail
Immediately updating the frontend UI as if the API mutation succeeded, and only reverting the change if the backend request subsequently fails
Displaying positive smiley face icons when forms submit
questions.explanation: Optimistic UI provides instant responsiveness (e.g., liking a post instantly toggles the heart icon), rolling back to the previous state with an error toast only if the network call rejects.

questions.question: How do you implement an API retry mechanism with Exponential Backoff in JavaScript?
options: Set `fetch(url, { retry: 'exponential' })`
Reload the entire browser window repeatedly until status is 200
Catch the error, wait for a progressively doubling delay (`Math.pow(2, attempt) * 1000ms`), and recursively re-call the fetch function up to max attempts
Send 100 requests simultaneously in a `while (true)` loop
questions.explanation: Exponential backoff delays retries by $2^{\text{attempt}} \times \text{baseDelay}$, preventing client retries from overwhelming recovering servers.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the HTTP `Authorization: Bearer <token>` header in REST API integration?
options: To specify which web browser model is sending the request
To authenticate the client by passing a signed JSON Web Token (JWT) or OAuth access token with each protected request
To authorize the server to charge the user's credit card
To bypass HTTPS encryption requirements on public Wi-Fi
questions.explanation: The `Authorization: Bearer <JWT>` header transmits authentication credentials securely on each API call for token-based authorization.

questions.question: What should an application do when an API responds with HTTP Status Code `401 Unauthorized`?
options: Display a 500 Internal Server Error page
Retry the exact same request 50 times in a loop
Attempt to refresh the access token using a refresh token, or redirect the user to the Login page to re-authenticate
Delete all HTML elements from the webpage
questions.explanation: `401 Unauthorized` indicates missing or expired authentication; modern apps intercept 401s, request a new token via refresh endpoint, and retry the original call.

questions.question: What is the difference between Polling and Server-Sent Events (SSE) for receiving live data updates from a backend?
options: Polling is full-duplex, while SSE is bidirectional
SSE only works in Node.js backends
Polling does not consume any network bandwidth
Polling repeatedly sends periodic HTTP requests on a timer, while SSE maintains a single persistent unidirectional HTTP connection streaming events from server to client
questions.explanation: Short/long polling incurs repeated HTTP overhead. Server-Sent Events (`EventSource`) establishes a persistent, low-overhead HTTP stream where the server pushes real-time updates.

questions.question: How can you read a Streaming API response (such as an LLM AI text generation stream) chunk-by-chunk using the Fetch API?
options: const stream = response.json(); while (stream.hasData()) { console.log(stream.next()); }
const reader = response.body.getReader(); const decoder = new TextDecoder(); while (true) { const { value, done } = await reader.read(); if (done) break; console.log(decoder.decode(value)); }
response.stream().forEach(chunk => console.log(chunk));
response.on('data', chunk => console.log(chunk));
questions.explanation: `response.body.getReader()` accesses the `ReadableStream` reader, allowing asynchronous decoding of streaming binary chunks (`Uint8Array`) using `TextDecoder` in real time.

questions.question: How do you cache an API response in `localStorage` with a 1-hour expiration timestamp?
options: Set `Cache-Control: max-age=3600` on `localStorage`
Store an object `{ data: apiResult, expiry: Date.now() + 3600000 }` stringified, and compare `Date.now() > item.expiry` before reading
localStorage.cache(url, apiResult, '1h');
localStorage.setItem(url, apiResult, { ttl: 3600 });
questions.explanation: `localStorage` has no native TTL; storing a wrapper object with an `expiry` timestamp allows checking if the cache is stale before making network requests.

questions.question: What causes a CORS (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing) error in the browser when making a `fetch()` request to an API?
options: The JavaScript code contains syntax errors in the JSON payload
The client computer does not have an active SSL certificate installed
The user's monitor refresh rate is lower than 60Hz
The server did not return an `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` header matching the client's origin protocol, domain, or port
questions.explanation: Browsers enforce the Same-Origin Policy; cross-origin requests are blocked unless the server explicitly sends `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` or `https://myclient.com`.

questions.question: What is the recommended method to build an Infinite Scroll pagination loader in pure JavaScript?
options: Load all 1,000,000 database records upfront on initial page load
Use `setInterval` polling every 500ms
Attach a synchronous `scroll` listener that recalculates document height every millisecond
Use an `IntersectionObserver` observing a sentinel element at the bottom of the feed to trigger fetching the next page when scrolled into view
questions.explanation: `IntersectionObserver` efficiently triggers page fetching when a target footer sentinel enters the viewport, avoiding scroll event layout thrashing.

questions.question: What does the `Accept: application/json` request header communicate to an API server?
options: It enables client-side database caching
It informs the server that the client expects and can process a response formatted in JSON
It informs the server of the data format contained in the request body
It forces the server to accept all uploaded files
questions.explanation: `Accept` specifies desired response MIME types (`application/json`), whereas `Content-Type` describes the MIME type of the sent request payload.

questions.question: How do you safely render dynamic text from an external API into a DOM container to prevent Cross-Site Scripting (XSS)?
options: document.write(apiData.title);
cardTitle.eval(apiData.title);
cardTitle.textContent = apiData.title; (or sanitize with DOMPurify before assigning to innerHTML)
cardTitle.innerHTML = apiData.title;
questions.explanation: Using `element.textContent` treats API strings strictly as text without HTML parsing, neutralizing any injected `<script>` or `onerror` tags.

questions.question: What HTTP Status Code is standard for a successful `DELETE` request that returns no content in the response body?
options: 204 No Content
202 Accepted
201 Created
200 OK
questions.explanation: Status code `204 No Content` indicates the server successfully fulfilled the request and there is no additional content to send in the response payload.

questions.question: What is the output of `JSON.stringify({ a: 1, b: undefined, c: null, d: NaN })`?
options: TypeError: NaN cannot be serialized
"{"a":1,"b":undefined,"c":null,"d":NaN}"
"{"a":1,"c":null,"d":null}"
questions.explanation: `undefined` properties are omitted, `null` remains `null`, and `NaN` (as well as `Infinity`) is converted to `null` in JSON serialization.
